passages.text: Loss of Nocturnal Dipping in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus According to Diabetic Kidney Disease: The Role of Vitamin D Levels

<bold>Background/Objectives:</bold> Abnormal nocturnal dipping (ND) in diabetes mellitus is linked to adverse outcomes. <sentence_start/>Its association with vitamin D (VD), cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN), and diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains unclear. <sentence_start/>We aim to evaluate the association of VD status with ND loss as well as CAN in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) across different DKD stages. <sentence_start/><bold>Methods:</bold> 83 T2DM patients were included in this cross-sectional study: 36 with early-stage DKD (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio [UACR] 30-299 mg/g; Group 1) as well as 47 with advanced-stage DKD (UACR ≥ 300 mg/g; Group 2). <sentence_start/><bold>Results:</bold> Patients with advanced DKD exhibited higher CAN prevalence (72.70% vs. 52.80%; <italic>p</italic> < 0.05), lower 25(OH)D (26.90 ± 9.90 vs. 29.60 ± 8.00 ng/mL; <italic>p</italic> = 0.05), and lower systolic ND (0.82 ± 8.40 vs. 4.50 ± 7%; <italic>p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/>Among patients with advanced DKD, lower 25(OH)D levels, classified according to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) criteria (normal ≥ 20 ng/mL), were associated with reduced systolic ND (1.90 ± 7.80 vs. −5.60 ± 9.30%; <italic>p</italic> < 0.05), while the Endocrine Society criteria showed a progressive reduction in systolic ND across VD classification (insufficiency 20-29.9, deficiency <20, and sufficiency ≥30 ng/mL), (−5.60 ± 9.30 vs. −0.20 ± 7.30 vs. 3.30 ± 8%, respectively; <italic>p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/>Patients with definite/severe CAN exhibited lower systolic ND (−4.38 ± 7.41 vs. 3.34 ± 8.00%; <italic>p</italic> < 0.01) than those with absent/early CAN. <sentence_start/>In addition, lower VD levels were associated with greater CAN severity according to both the Endocrine Society criteria (<italic>p</italic> < 0.01, r = 0.40), and the IOM criteria (<italic>p</italic> < 0.05, r = 0.30). <sentence_start/>In the regression model, VD remained an independent predictor of absence of diastolic ND (Rsqr = 0.393; <italic>p</italic> < 0.05). <sentence_start/><bold>Conclusions:</bold> These findings suggest a potential link between vitamin D status, autonomic dysfunction, and ND in patients with T2DM and advanced DKD.
1. Introduction

Nocturnal dipping (ND) corresponds to the physiological reduction in blood pressure (BP) during sleep and represents one of the main parameters used to assess circadian BP behavior [<citation rid="B1-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0000000000000221" pmid="24886823" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="B2-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0000000000003480" pmid="37345492" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="B3-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178" pmid="39210715" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0000000000004053" pmid="40509714" pmcid="PMC12237141" count="1">4</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A nighttime drop in blood pressure of at least 10% defines the dipper pattern according to ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) [<citation rid="B2-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0000000000003480" pmid="37345492" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="B3-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/eurheartj/ehae178" pmid="39210715" count="1">3</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Abnormal ND, defined as a ND reduction of less than 10%, has been related with the development of kidney disease and also adverse cardiovascular outcomes in individuals affected by diabetes [<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00041552-200109000-00010" pmid="11496054" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa013410" pmid="12226150" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/07420520903044448" pmid="19637052" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep34932" pmid="27713498" pmcid="PMC5054683" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B9-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/jdi.12691" pmcid="PMC5835479" pmid="28494142" count="1">9</citation>,<citation rid="B10-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2174/1573402114666180607090205" pmid="29875006" Among the factors potentially involved in impaired ND, diabetic kidney disease (DKD) and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN) have received particular attention. <sentence_start/>DKD, characterized by progressive renal dysfunction, albuminuria, and impaired vitamin D activation [<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018" pmid="38490803" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="B13-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/medicina55060273" pmid="31200589" pmcid="PMC6630278" count="1">13</citation>,<citation rid="B14-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.eclnm.2010.05.001" count="1">14</citation>], has been increasingly recognized as an important contributor to disruption of the physiological circadian BP pattern, including reduced ND and a higher frequency of nocturnal hypertension in people who have diabetes [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa013410" pmid="12226150" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep34932" pmid="27713498" pmcid="PMC5054683" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1464-5491.1999.00127.x" pmid="10445830" count="1">15</citation>,<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02807" progression, suggesting a bidirectional relationship between renal dysfunction and circadian BP abnormalities [<citation rid="B18-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1475-2840-5-19" pmid="18650998" pmcid="PMC2323760" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In parallel, CAN, characterized by the Toronto Consensus as impairment of cardiovascular autonomic control in diabetes, is associated with sympathetic overactivity and reduced heart rate variability [<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.4093/dmj.2018.0259" pmid="30793549" pmcid="PMC6387879" reverse-dipping and non-dipping patterns in individuals affected by diabetes [<citation rid="B22-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2337/diacare.17.6.578" pmid="8082528" count="1">22</citation>,<citation rid="B23-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/sj.jhh.1001170" pmid="11319671" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="B24-nutrients-18-02807" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41440-018-0130-5" pmid="30401911" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-024-56934-1" pmid="38493259" pmcid="PMC10944468" count="1">27</citation>]. <sentence_start/>CAN and DKD appear to be closely interconnected complications of diabetes [<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dmrr.1239" pmid="21695768" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.diabres.2021.109181" pmid="34952039" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2024.1462610" pmcid="PMC11424464" pmid="39329106" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2026.1810159" pmcid="PMC13124521" pmid="42064771" count="1">31</citation>].

Furthermore, vitamin D deficiency has been identified as a possible cause of both renal and autonomic dysfunction in diabetes, with lower 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D) levels associated with DKD progression, higher levels of albuminuria as well as a higher prevalence of CAN [<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41598-024-56934-1" pmid="38493259" pmcid="PMC10944468" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2026.1810159" pmcid="PMC13124521" pmid="42064771" reported a connection between lower serum vitamin D levels, the existence of CAN, and absence of ND, as well as improvements in autonomic parameters following vitamin D supplementation [<citation Despite evidence linking vitamin D deficiency to DKD, CAN, and impaired ND regulation, the interplay among these factors across the spectrum of DKD remains poorly understood. <sentence_start/>Based on the available literature, no previous study has simultaneously evaluated vitamin D levels, CAN severity, as well as ND in individuals with Type 2 DM (T2DM) according to the DKD stage.
2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Study Design and Patients

A cross-sectional study was conducted to investigate the relationship among serum VD levels, CAN, as well as ABPM findings, including nocturnal dipping status and blood pressure variability, in individuals with T2DM at both early and advanced phases of DKD. <sentence_start/>A total of 83 participants receiving regular care at the Endocrinology Department of the João de Barros Barreto University Hospital (HUJBB), Federal University of Pará (UFPA), were enrolled between 2023 and 2025. <sentence_start/>Participants were categorized based on urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) values in an early DKD group (30-299 mg/g; <italic>n</italic> = 36), corresponding to KDIGO 2022 stage A2, and an advanced DKD group (≥300 mg/g; <italic>n</italic> = 47), corresponding to stage A3. <sentence_start/>The study protocol complied with the ethical principles established by the Declaration of Helsinki (2008 revision) as well as the Nuremberg Code and received approval from the HUJBB Research Ethics Committee (number of reference 88974918.6.0000.0017). <sentence_start/>All participants signed an Informed Consent Form (ICF). <sentence_start/>Eligibility criteria included: (a) signing the ICF before the study participation; (b) T2DM diagnosis and age ≥30 with routine endocrinologist follow-up; (c) stable therapy using glucose-lowering oral agents and/or using therapy with insulin for a minimum of three months; (d) presence of DKD with UACR ≥ 30 mg/g; (e) 25 to 90 mL/min/1.73 m<sup>2</sup> as the estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR); (f) steady dosages of every drug for a minimum of four weeks before the screening appointment; and (g) capacity and willingness to comply with all study procedures, attend scheduled visits, and complete the study.

Exclusion criteria were: (a) type 1 diabetes mellitus or other types of diabetes; (b) bone metabolism diseases; (c) previous hepatic disease; (d) taking vitamin D as well as calcium supplementation in the past three months prior to screening; (e) uncompensated hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism; (f) lactation, pregnancy, or the intention to become pregnant; (g) diseases that, at the researcher’s discretion, could interfere with life expectancy; and (h) abuse of recreational drugs or alcohol that may interfere with study procedures or participant safety.
2.2. <sentence_start/>Data Collection

Following eligibility assessment, participants underwent clinical, laboratory, and blood pressure evaluations during scheduled visits at the Clinical Research Department of HUJBB. <sentence_start/>Demographic data, medical history, use of medication, as well as anthropometric metrics (mass, stature, and body mass index) were collected. <sentence_start/>The diagnosis of T2DM followed established clinical and laboratory criteria [<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2337/dc26-S002" pmid="39651986" pmcid="PMC11635041" count="1">51</citation>].

Serum 25(OH)D levels were assessed by the DiaSorin LIAISON<sup>®</sup> chemiluminescence method (DiaSorin, Stillwater, MN, USA) [<citation rid="B52-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" count="1">52</citation>], a technique validated via the Vitamin D External Quality Assessment Scheme (DEQAS), a widely used international external quality assessment program for vitamin D testing. <sentence_start/>Glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) was determined by efficient liquid chromatography (HPLC) [<citation rid="B53-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16278773" pmcid="PMC1240025" count="1">53</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Fasting plasma glucose, albumin, lipid profile, and triglycerides were analyzed by automated colorimetric techniques. <sentence_start/>Serum creatinine was determined by an automated kinetic method, and albuminuria was measured by immunoturbidimetry [<citation rid="B54-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fphys.2022.937701" pmid="35846022" pmcid="PMC9281578" count="1">54</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The GFR was calculated with the CKD-EPI formula, without race adjustment [<citation rid="B55-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa2102953" pmid="34554658" pmcid="PMC8822996" count="1">55</citation>].
2.3. <sentence_start/>Classification of DKD

UACR was assessed three times in all patients, with each measurement occurring at different time intervals. <sentence_start/>For DKD classification, two categories were considered: moderately increased (UACR 30-299 mg/g) and significantly increased albuminuria (UACR ≥ 300 mg/g) [<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018" pmid="38490803" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Patients were categorized based on the classification identified in at least two of the three measurements. <sentence_start/>For consistency and clarity during the manuscript, participants exhibiting moderately elevated and significantly elevated albuminuria were categorized as having early and advanced phases of diabetic kidney disease, respectively.
2.4. <sentence_start/>Vitamin D Assessment

Serum 25(OH)D concentrations were categorized based on two reference guidelines: the Institute of Medicine (IOM) [<citation rid="B56-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jocd.2011.03.004" pmid="21787514" count="1">56</citation>], which categorizes 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels into deficiency (<20 ng/mL) and sufficiency (≥20 ng/mL), and the historical 2011 Endocrine Society criteria [<citation rid="B57-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/jc.2011-0385" pmid="21646368" count="1">57</citation>], that stratify 25(OH)D serum levels into insufficiency (20-29.90 ng/mL), deficiency (<20 ng/mL), and sufficiency (≥30 ng/mL).
2.5. <sentence_start/>Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM)

The oscillometric method was used for ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) with a validated portable monitor (Oscar 2 ABPM SphygmoCor<sup>®</sup>), with measurements taken every 15 min over a 24 h period. <sentence_start/>Instructions were given to the participants to keep their routine and to register their sleep as well as wake periods. <sentence_start/>Mean systolic and diastolic BP (SBP and DBP) values were obtained for the 24 h, during the waking and sleeping periods. <sentence_start/>ABPM has previously demonstrated good reproducibility in patients with T2DM [<citation rid="B58-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12664504" count="1">58</citation>,<citation rid="B59-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1590/S0066-782X2007000200012" pmid="17384839" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The examination was considered valid when ≥70% of the scheduled measurements were successfully obtained. <sentence_start/>Morning blood pressure was defined as the average of the measurements obtained during the first two hours after awakening [<citation rid="B60-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.119.14233" pmid="32008430" pmcid="PMC7035156" count="1">60</citation>].

Nocturnal dipping (ND) was determined through the percentage reduction in blood pressure during sleep relative to the daytime period, using the following well-established and standard formula Systolic or diastolic nocturnal dipping: (%) = [(mean waking SBP/DBP − mean sleeping SBP/DPB)/mean waking SBP] × 100 [<citation rid="B59-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1590/S0066-782X2007000200012" pmid="17384839" count="1">59</citation>,<citation rid="B61-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/HYP.0000000000000087" pmcid="PMC11409525" pmid="30827125" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Participants were classified as reverse dipper (<0%), non-dipper (0-10%), dipper (10-20%), and extreme dipper (>20%) [<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/srep34932" pmid="27713498" pmcid="PMC5054683" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For additional analyses, individuals were also grouped in two more patterns: loss of ND (ND < 0%) and presence of ND (ND > 0%).
2.6. CAN Assessment

Autonomic functional testing was conducted in the morning following verification of capillary glucose concentrations between 70 and 250 mg/dL. <sentence_start/>Participants were instructed to avoid alcoholic beverages, caffeine, as well as smoking for at least 8 h and vigorous physical activity for 24 h prior to testing. <sentence_start/>Cases of fever (>37.80 °C), significant emotional stress, or recent hypoglycemia resulted in rescheduling of the examination. <sentence_start/>The VNS-Micro<sup>®</sup> system (Neurosoft LLC, Ivanovo, Russia) was used.

Cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CARTs) served as the reference standard in line with the Toronto Consensus, which included deep breathing (E:I ratio), the Valsalva maneuver, and the orthostatic test (30:15 ratio and assessment of orthostatic hypotension) [<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dmrr.1239" pmid="21695768" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For the Valsalva maneuver, the patient sustained an expiratory strain of 40 mmHg for 15 s while lying supine under continuous electrocardiographic tracking. <sentence_start/>The 30:15 test evaluated the relationship between early heart rate elevation and subsequent reflexive deceleration following the change to the standing position. <sentence_start/>The deep breathing test consisted of determining the E:I ratio during controlled respiratory cycles. <sentence_start/>Diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension required a fall of ≥20 mmHg in systolic blood pressure and/or ≥10 mmHg in diastolic blood pressure within a 3 min standing interval. <sentence_start/>Time-domain indices of heart rate variability (HRV) were gathered in supine patients through the VNS-Micro<sup>®</sup> platform (Neurosoft LLC, Ivanovo, Russia) [<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/bf02322053" pmid="11570610" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>For spectral analysis, participants remained elevated in the supine position at 30° and breathing spontaneously during a 300 s ECG recording. <sentence_start/>Signals were digitally transformed using mathematical algorithms, generating amplitude-versus-frequency spectra.

The following spectral bands were evaluated: very low frequency (VLF: 0.01-0.04 Hz), representing vasomotor sympathetic activity and body temperature regulation; low frequency (LF: 0.04-0.15 Hz), associated with sympathetic-vagal baroreflex modulation; as well as high frequency (HF: 0.15-0.5 Hz), considered a marker of parasympathetic activity. <sentence_start/>In the time domain, RRmin, RRmax, RRNN, and SDNN were analyzed. <sentence_start/>Frequency-domain parameters included VLF, LF, HF, total power (TP), alongside the LF/HF ratio, used as an indicator of sympathovagal balance.

Interpretation of HRV parameters followed the reference values proposed by [<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/bf02322053" pmid="11570610" count="1">62</citation>], which should be considered estimates without validated clinical cutoff points. <sentence_start/>Identification of CAN followed the framework outlined by the Toronto Consensus criteria. <sentence_start/>For CAN staging, classification was based on the number of abnormal Ewing tests and the presence or absence of orthostatic hypotension. <sentence_start/>Patients without evidence of CAN were defined by normal test results. <sentence_start/>Early CAN was defined by one abnormal heart rate test (or borderline results), whereas definite CAN was diagnosed upon the detection of two or more abnormal tests. <sentence_start/>Severe CAN was diagnosed in the presence of orthostatic hypotension associated with at least one abnormal autonomic test [<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dmrr.1239" pmid="21695768" count="1">21</citation>].
2.7. <sentence_start/>Statistical Analysis

Computational processing was conducted using SigmaPlot 12.0<sup>®</sup> (Systat Software Inc., San Jose, CA, USA) alongside Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS version 22, IBM Corp., Chicago, IL, USA). <sentence_start/>A <italic>p</italic> value < 0.05 was defined as statistically significant throughout all evaluations.

Qualitative data were summarized as absolute frequencies accompanied by percentages (%). <sentence_start/>Quantitative data are presented as mean ± standard deviation when normally distributed and as median and interquartile range (25th-75th percentile) when non-normally distributed. <sentence_start/>The distribution of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test.

For comparative analyses of continuous variables between the early-stage and advanced-stage DKD groups, Student’s independent-samples <italic>t</italic>-test was used for normally distributed variables, whereas the Mann-Whitney U test was used for variables with a non-normal distribution. <sentence_start/>The same approach was applied to other analyses involving two independent groups, including comparisons of ABPM parameters according to the Institute of Medicine vitamin D classification (25[OH]D < 20 vs. ≥20 ng/mL), comparisons between patients with absent/early versus definite/severe cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN), and comparisons between reverse dippers and participants with other nocturnal dipping patterns.

For analyses involving three independent groups, specifically comparisons of ABPM parameters across the historical 2011 Endocrine Society vitamin D categories (sufficiency, ≥30 ng/mL; insufficiency, 20-29.9 ng/mL; and deficiency, <20 ng/mL), one-way ANOVA was used when the assumptions of normality were satisfied, whereas the Kruskal-Wallis test was used for non-normally distributed variables.

Associations between categorical variables, including the comparison of clinical characteristics, comorbidities, medication use, CAN prevalence, and nocturnal dipping categories between DKD groups, were evaluated using the chi-square test. <sentence_start/>Fisher’s exact test was used instead when the assumptions of the chi-square test were not met because of small expected cell frequencies.

Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to investigate whether serum 25(OH)D concentration was independently associated with reverse-dipping status. <sentence_start/>Reverse dipping was entered as the dependent binary variable (reverse dipper = 1; non-dipper, dipper, and extreme dipper = 0), and serum 25(OH)D concentration was entered as the main independent variable. <sentence_start/>The multivariable model was adjusted for potential confounding factors, including age, duration of T2DM, HbA1c, eGFR, lipid profile, blood pressure levels, and the use of ACE inhibitors/angiotensin II receptor blockers, SGLT2 inhibitors, beta-blockers, and GLP-1 receptor agonists.

Sample power and size were calculated according to the primary study hypothesis evaluating the relationship between serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels and nocturnal blood pressure dipping. <sentence_start/>Considering an expected Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.30, a two-sided significance level of 5% (α = 0.05), and a statistical power of 80% (1 − β), the minimum required sample size was estimated to be 70 participants. <sentence_start/>Sample size calculations were performed using SigmaPlot version 12.0.
3. Results

A total of 83 individuals took part in the study, with their main clinical and demographic data detailed in Table 1. <sentence_start/>Participants were divided into an early DKD stage (30-299 mg/g; <italic>n</italic> = 36) and an advanced DKD stage (≥300 mg/g; <italic>n</italic> = 47). <sentence_start/>The comparisons were performed between these groups. <sentence_start/>As expected, patients with advanced DKD were older and exhibited a longer history of T2DM. <sentence_start/>Notably, all participants in the advanced DKD group were receiving SGLT2 inhibitors. <sentence_start/>In addition, they exhibited a greater burden of diabetes-related complications, including a higher CAN prevalence.

Table 2 shows a laboratory profile consistent with the greater severity of renal dysfunction observed in patients with advanced DKD, including higher serum creatinine and UACR levels and lower GFR values. <sentence_start/>In addition, these patients showed significantly decreased circulating 25(OH)D levels compared to subjects with early-stage DKD, in conjunction with a less favorable lipid profile, characterized by elevated total cholesterol.

BP parameters obtained from 24 h ABPM are presented in Table 3. <sentence_start/>Patients with advanced-stage DKD exhibited higher SBP levels throughout the 24 h period, including daytime, nighttime, and morning intervals, along with reduced nocturnal systolic BP dipping. <sentence_start/>Importantly, mean nocturnal systolic BP dipping in this group fell within a non-dipper range.

The blood pressure parameters presented above were further grouped according to 25(OH)D levels according to guidelines from the Institute of Medicine (IOM) as well as the Endocrine Society (Table 4 and Table 5). <sentence_start/>Similar results were obtained using both classification systems. <sentence_start/>Among participants with advanced-stage DKD, lower circulating VD levels were associated with reduced nocturnal SBP dipping, and a trend toward a lower nocturnal DBP dipping, whereas no such correlation was found in patients with early-stage DKD. <sentence_start/>No significant differences were found for the remaining BP variables across VD categories.

At the advanced-DKD stage, patients were categorized as reverse dippers (<italic>n</italic> = 16; 34%), non-dippers (<italic>n</italic> = 18; 38.30%), dippers (<italic>n</italic> = 11; 23.40%), or extreme dippers (<italic>n</italic> = 2; 4.30%) according to ND status. <sentence_start/>In this group, compared with the other dipping patterns, reverse dippers showed lower serum 25(OH)D concentrations (26.70 ± 9.30 vs. 30.90 ± 7.60, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05) and higher triglyceride levels (303 ± 205 vs. 190.40 ± 104, <italic>p</italic> < 0.05).

In the early-stage DKD group, nine patients (25%) were classified as reverse dippers, 18 (50%) as non-dippers, nine (25%) as dippers, and none as extreme dippers. <sentence_start/>The distribution of nocturnal dipping patterns did not differ significantly between the early- and advanced-stage DKD groups (<italic>p</italic> = 0.43).

BP parameters according to CAN severity, classified based on the Toronto Consensus criteria, are presented in Table 6. <sentence_start/>Among patients with advanced-stage DKD, those with definite/severe CAN (<italic>n</italic> = 19; 40.43%) exhibited significantly lower systolic and diastolic ND values, compared with patients with absent/early CAN (<italic>n</italic> = 28; 59.57%). <sentence_start/>Notably, patients with definite/severe CAN exhibited a systolic reverse-dipper pattern. <sentence_start/>The remaining ambulatory monitoring parameters did not differ significantly between study groups.

4. Discussion

Our results show an association between lower serum vitamin D (VD) concentrations, presence and intensity of cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (CAN), and impaired nocturnal dipping (ND) in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and advanced diabetic kidney disease (DKD). <sentence_start/>Only in this group, a progressive decline in nocturnal systolic blood pressure (SBP) dipping was observed as vitamin D status worsened, regardless of whether vitamin D status was classified according to Institute of Medicine or Endocrine Society criteria. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, individuals with definite/severe CAN exhibited lower systolic and diastolic ND values compared with those with absent/early CAN. <sentence_start/>Lower vitamin D concentrations were also associated with both greater CAN severity and reduced nocturnal diastolic blood pressure (BP) dipping, as demonstrated by correlation analyses. <sentence_start/>Notably, serum vitamin D concentration remained an independent predictor of diastolic reverse dipping after adjustment for potential confounding factors.

Abnormal ND patterns have frequently been correlated with a higher risk of cardiovascular and renal events and have been recognized as a marker of adverse prognosis [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1475-2840-9-36" pmid="20704750" pmcid="PMC2928765" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B63-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/00004872-200211000-00017" pmid="12409956" count="1">63</citation>,<citation rid="B64-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1161/HYPERTENSIONAHA.119.14085" pmid="31865788" count="1">64</citation>,<citation rid="B65-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41371-026-01160-7" pmid="42156868" pmcid="PMC13345891" count="1">65</citation>,<citation rid="B66-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm15062374" pmid="41899304" pmcid="PMC13026712" count="1">66</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similar associations have been reported in populations with T2DM and DKD [<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/07420520903044448" pmid="19637052" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B10-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2174/1573402114666180607090205" pmid="29875006" pmcid="PMC6635654" count="1">10</citation>,<citation rid="B67-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/dom.14798" pmid="35676796" pmcid="PMC9796931" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40200-023-01337-8" pmid="38932843" pmcid="PMC11196480" count="1">68</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Recently, Chiriacò et al. (2022), in a retrospective cohort study involving 349 patients with diabetes mellitus, demonstrated that reverse-dipper pattern was associated with reduced survival and a twofold increase in all-cause mortality [<citation rid="B67-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/dom.14798" pmid="35676796" pmcid="PMC9796931" count="1">67</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Likewise, Akintunde et al. (2024), in a cross-sectional study with 100 T2DM patients, reported associations between non-dipping and reverse-dipping patterns and markers of increased cardiovascular risk, including impaired kidney function [<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40200-023-01337-8" pmid="38932843" pmcid="PMC11196480" count="1">68</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In light of these findings, ABPM remains the reference method for assessing 24 h BP behavior, enabling the detection of abnormalities in ND and sleep-time BP that are not identified by office measurements and that provide important prognostic information. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, characterization of ND patterns may improve renal and cardiovascular risk assessment in patients with diabetes.

As expected, patients with early-stage DKD exhibited a lower frequency of diabetes-related complications and less severe renal impairment compared with those with advanced DKD. <sentence_start/>Although participants with early-stage DKD also presented a high prevalence of the non-dipper pattern, consistent with previous studies reporting alterations in nocturnal dipping behavior in this population [<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0002-9343(97)00051-X" pmid="9217667" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41371-021-00587-4" pmid="34400769" count="1">70</citation>], the association among reduced ND, lower vitamin D concentrations, and the presence of CAN was not significant in the setting of early renal disease. <sentence_start/>These results might reflect the lower degree of renal and autonomic impairment in these individuals, as abnormalities in blood pressure regulation and cardiovascular autonomic function tend to become more pronounced with DKD progression [<citation rid="B2-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0000000000003480" pmid="37345492" count="1">2</citation>,<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.kint.2023.10.018" pmid="38490803" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/dmrr.1239" pmid="21695768" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B71-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrcardio.2013.1" pmid="23399972" count="1">71</citation>].

Abnormal nocturnal dipping patterns have consistently been reported in individuals with diabetes and greater renal impairment, characterized by increased albuminuria and a less favorable BP profile compared with the dipper pattern [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa013410" pmid="12226150" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1464-5491.1999.00127.x" pmid="10445830" count="1">15</citation>,<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0b013e3282f06428" pmid="17984670" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1475-2840-9-36" pmid="20704750" pmcid="PMC2928765" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0002-9343(97)00051-X" pmid="9217667" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B72-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1474651408096678" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>More recent evidence has further linked progression of renal injury to increased BP variability [<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1753-0407.70160" pmid="41126798" pmcid="PMC12547349" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a prospective study of individuals with T1DM and initially normal albumin excretion, Lurbe et al. demonstrated that elevated sleep-time systolic BP preceded the development of microalbuminuria [<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmoa013410" pmid="12226150" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In parallel, Felício et al. (2010) also described similar results in T2DM [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1475-2840-9-36" pmid="20704750" pmcid="PMC2928765" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Finally, studies in T2DM have reported a higher prevalence of albuminuria among patients with a systolic non-dipper pattern [<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/hjh.0b013e3282f06428" pmid="17984670" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0002-9343(97)00051-X" pmid="9217667" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B72-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/1474651408096678" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>From a pathophysiological perspective, persistent sympathetic activation during sleep, reflected by increased norepinephrine levels, may contribute to the maintenance of vascular resistance and elevated BP in patients with diabetic nephropathy [<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1464-5491.1999.00127.x" pmid="10445830" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In addition, sodium dysregulation, fluid retention and persistent activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), commonly observed in DKD, may promote volume overload and sustained nocturnal hypertension [<citation rid="B73-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/s1043-2760(03)00111-5" pmid="12890592" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consistent with these observations, patients with advanced DKD in our study exhibited higher systolic BP levels throughout the 24 h period, along with reduced nocturnal systolic BP dipping compatible with a non-dipper profile. <sentence_start/>Collectively, these findings support the association between adverse ND behavior and greater severity of renal involvement in diabetes mellitus.

The primary limitation of the present study is the relatively limited sample size, and larger studies are necessary to confirm the results. <sentence_start/>Additionally, due to its cross-sectional design, causal relationships among serum vitamin D concentrations, CAN, and ND cannot be established, and reverse causality cannot be excluded. <sentence_start/>All T2DM patients were followed in the Endocrinology Department of our University Hospital and had their physical activity and dietary intake previously standardized according to the American Diabetes Association guidelines [<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2337/dc26-S002" pmid="39651986" pmcid="PMC11635041" count="1">51</citation>], thereby minimizing the influence of those factors. <sentence_start/>However, individual sun exposure duration was not assessed. <sentence_start/>Despite year-round exposure to relatively intense solar radiation in our region, previous studies suggest that sunlight alone may not ensure adequate vitamin D status, as insufficiency and deficiency can also occur in areas with abundant sunlight [<citation rid="B103-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s40520-020-01570-8" pmid="32377965" pmcid="PMC7202265" count="1">103</citation>,<citation rid="B104-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.26719/2011.17.4.317" pmid="22259890" count="1">104</citation>,<citation rid="B105-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1056/nejmra070553" pmid="17634462" count="1">105</citation>,<citation rid="B106-nutrients-18-02807" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1359/jbmr.2000.15.9.1856" pmid="10977006" count="1">106</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Additionally, the universal use of SGLT2 inhibitors among patients with clinical DKD represents a potential confounding factor, as the effect of SGLT2 inhibitors on BP and ND could not be independently assessed due to the absence of variability in treatment exposure across DKD stages.

On the other hand, a major strength of this study is the population uniformity, classified based on DKD stages, with the exclusion of patients undergoing dialysis or in the pre-dialysis stage. <sentence_start/>Additional strengths include the use of standardized criteria for CAN diagnosis and rigorous validation of ABPM recordings.

Future prospective longitudinal studies are needed to establish the temporal relationship among vitamin D status, impaired nocturnal dipping, CAN, and DKD progression. <sentence_start/>Larger multicenter studies may help confirm these associations across different stages of kidney and autonomic dysfunction. <sentence_start/>Moreover, randomized controlled trials investigating whether correction of vitamin D deficiency improves nocturnal blood pressure regulation or autonomic function would be required to determine whether vitamin D has a causal or potentially modifiable role in these abnormalities.

Overall, our results indicate that VD deficiency and the presence of CAN may represent interconnected pathways associated with impaired ND, particularly in advanced stages of DKD. <sentence_start/>From a clinical perspective, these findings emphasize the significance of a comprehensive cardiovascular assessment in these patients, including the evaluation of CAN and abnormalities in nocturnal dipping patterns, together with biochemical markers such as vitamin D levels, to improve stratification of cardiovascular risk in this group of patients.
5. Conclusions

To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to simultaneously explore the associations among vitamin D concentrations, CAN, and ND across DKD stages in T2DM. <sentence_start/>Lower serum vitamin D levels and CAN were linked to a higher prevalence of non-dipping in patients with T2DM and advanced DKD. <sentence_start/>These associations were not observed in early stages, suggesting a stage-dependent interaction between vitamin D status, autonomic dysfunction, and ND. <sentence_start/>These results highlight ABPM and vitamin D measurement as valuable tools in the assessment of advanced DKD. <sentence_start/>Although causal inference cannot be established, our results suggest that vitamin D deficiency and autonomic dysfunction may represent interconnected pathways contributing to altered nocturnal blood pressure control and higher cardiovascular risk in this population. <sentence_start/>Larger longitudinal studies are necessary to confirm our findings.
